lab.title: Verify the cumulative async clock-in workflow
lab.objective: Exercise AsyncClockEntryService with the real EF repository and SQLite.
lab.task: Prove one clock-in is persisted and a second open clock-in is rejected without changing database state.
lab.startingCondition: Sessions 26–30 prepared Task and DI concepts; Sessions 31–34B created real SQLite persistence, query execution, an HTTP boundary, verified registrations, and deliberate API errors. Session 35 tests the natural duplicate-clock-in rule across those boundaries.

steps.text: Step 1/12: In the test project, create ClockEntryWorkflowTests.cs and declare public sealed class ClockEntryWorkflowTests.
Step 2/12: Add async Fact TryClockInAsync_PersistsOnceAndRejectsADuplicateOpenEntry returning Task.
Step 3/12: Inside Arrange, create and open one in-memory SqliteConnection. Keep it open for the whole test so the database survives across contexts and commands.
Step 4/12: Create DbContextOptions<TimeClockDbContext> with UseSqlite(connection), construct the context, and await EnsureCreatedAsync.
Step 5/12: Construct EfClockEntryRepository and AsyncClockEntryService using that real context.
Step 6/12: Choose fixed employee ID 35 and a fixed clock-in DateTime.
Step 7/12: Inside Act, await TryClockInAsync once and store firstAttempt.
Step 8/12: Await TryClockInAsync again for the same employee and store secondAttempt.
Step 9/12: Assert firstAttempt is true and secondAttempt is false. false represents the expected duplicate-open-entry rejection.
Step 10/12: Await dbContext.ClockEntries.CountAsync and assert the database still contains exactly one row.
Step 11/12: Run ClockEntryWorkflowTests and review the passing result.
Step 12/12: Run ScratchPad and App, start Web to verify startup, build the full Release solution, and run every test with --no-build.

reveals.title: Solution
reveals.text: The integration test proves success, expected duplicate rejection, and unchanged row count.
